claim: UBE2O is a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Here, we report the identification of ubiquitin conjugating enzyme E2 O (UBE2O), a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase (Mashtalir et al., 2014; Vila et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013a), as being critical for Tat transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mashtalir et al., 2014; Vila et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013a).

claim: UBE2O is critical for Tat transcriptional activity.
source: Here, we report the identification of ubiquitin conjugating enzyme E2 O (UBE2O), a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase (Mashtalir et al., 2014; Vila et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013a), as being critical for Tat transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including RNAi knockdown experiments showing reduced Tat activity (Figure 1A).

claim: Tat recruits UBE2O to robustly ubiquitinate HEXIM1 in a non-degradative manner.
source: We show that Tat recruits UBE2O to robustly ubiquitinate HEXIM1 in a non-degradative manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including ubiquitination assays (Figure 3) and proteasome inhibitor experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: UBE2O-dependent ubiquitinated HEXIM1 species are largely cytoplasmic.
source: Interestingly, UBE2O-dependent ubiquitinated HEXIM1 species are largely cytoplasmic, which led to the discovery of a cytoplasmic pool of P-TEFb-7SK snRNP.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments showing ubiquitinated HEXIM1 in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 5B).

claim: A cytoplasmic pool of P-TEFb-7SK snRNP exists.
source: Interestingly, UBE2O-dependent ubiquitinated HEXIM1 species are largely cytoplasmic, which led to the discovery of a cytoplasmic pool of P-TEFb-7SK snRNP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including subcellular fractionation and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7A).

claim: Tat-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination by UBE2O releases P-TEFb from the cytoplasmic reservoir with the 7SK snRNP.
source: Tat-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination by UBE2O releases P-TEFb from this cytoplasmic reservoir with the 7SK snRNP, resulting in the nuclear import of the active kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing P-TEFb redistribution upon Tat expression (Figure 7D) and UBE2O-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination (Figure 3E).

claim: UBE2O activity is essential for Tat-dependent recruitment of P-TEFb to the viral promoter.
source: Further, UBE2O activity is essential for the Tat-dependent recruitment of P-TEFb to the viral promoter, demonstrating the importance of this ubiquitin ligase in targeting P-TEFb to chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing reduced CDK9 recruitment to the HIV-1 promoter upon UBE2O knockdown (Figure 7E).

claim: Treatment of cells with the CDK9 inhibitor DRB results in P-TEFb nuclear import and chromatin retention.
source: Finally, this mechanism of transcription elongation control appears to be more broadly used as treatment of cells with the CDK9 inhibitor, DRB, similarly resulted in P-TEFb nuclear import and chromatin retention with an increased association between UBE2O and HEXIM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments showing P-TEFb redistribution upon DRB treatment (Figure 8A).

claim: DRB treatment increases the association between UBE2O and HEXIM1.
source: Finally, this mechanism of transcription elongation control appears to be more broadly used as treatment of cells with the CDK9 inhibitor, DRB, similarly resulted in P-TEFb nuclear import and chromatin retention with an increased association between UBE2O and HEXIM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing increased HEXIM1 binding to UBE2O upon DRB treatment (Figure 8B).

claim: Many genes in higher eukaryotes contain stably paused RNAP II molecules immediately downstream of transcription start sites.
source: The advent of genome-wide methods to interrogate transcription has shown that many genes in higher eukaryotes contain stably paused RNAP II molecules immediately downstream of transcription start sites (Core et al., 2008; Henriques et al., 2013; Kwak and Lis, 2013; Rahl et al., 2010; Zeitlinger et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Core et al., 2008; Henriques et al., 2013; Kwak and Lis, 2013; Rahl et al., 2010; Zeitlinger et al., 2007).

claim: P-TEFb is composed of cyclin T1 (CCNT1) and cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) subunits.
source: The release of RNAP II into productive elongation is controlled by the kinase positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), composed of cyclin T1 (CCNT1) and cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) subunits (Kwak and Lis, 2013; Marshall and Price, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kwak and Lis, 2013; Marshall and Price, 1995).

claim: P-TEFb hyper-phosphorylates DSIF, NELF, and the C-terminal domain of RNAP II, resulting in a processive polymerase.
source: P-TEFb hyper-phosphorylates DRB sensitivity inducting factor (DSIF), negative elongation factor (NELF), and the C-terminal domain of RNAP II, resulting in a processive polymerase (Czudnochowski et al., 2012; Yamaguchi et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Czudnochowski et al., 2012; Yamaguchi et al., 1999).

claim: BRD4 interacts with P-TEFb to relieve pausing.
source: Numerous cellular proteins interact with P-TEFb to relieve pausing, including bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) (Yang et al., 2005), Mediator (Takahashi et al., 2011), nuclear factor (NF)-κB (Barboric et al., 2001), and c-Myc (Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2005).

claim: Mediator interacts with P-TEFb to relieve pausing.
source: Numerous cellular proteins interact with P-TEFb to relieve pausing, including bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) (Yang et al., 2005), Mediator (Takahashi et al., 2011), nuclear factor (NF)-κB (Barboric et al., 2001), and c-Myc (Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Takahashi et al., 2011).

claim: NF-κB interacts with P-TEFb to relieve pausing.
source: Numerous cellular proteins interact with P-TEFb to relieve pausing, including bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) (Yang et al., 2005), Mediator (Takahashi et al., 2011), nuclear factor (NF)-κB (Barboric et al., 2001), and c-Myc (Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Barboric et al., 2001).

claim: c-Myc interacts with P-TEFb to relieve pausing.
source: Numerous cellular proteins interact with P-TEFb to relieve pausing, including bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) (Yang et al., 2005), Mediator (Takahashi et al., 2011), nuclear factor (NF)-κB (Barboric et al., 2001), and c-Myc (Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002).

claim: HIV-1 Tat interacts with P-TEFb to activate a paused polymerase at the viral promoter.
source: The human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) transcription factor, Tat, also interacts with P-TEFb to activate a paused polymerase at the viral promoter (Feinberg et al., 1991; Wei et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Feinberg et al., 1991; Wei et al., 1998).

claim: P-TEFb activity is controlled by sequestration into the inhibitory 7SK snRNP complex.
source: P-TEFb activity is controlled by sequestration into the inhibitory 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex (Nguyen et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nguyen et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001).

claim: HEXIM1 inhibits the kinase activity of CDK9 in a 7SK snRNA-dependent manner.
source: In this complex, hexamethylene bisacetamide inducible 1 (HEXIM1) inhibits the kinase activity of CDK9 in a 7SK snRNA-dependent manner (Michels et al., 2004), while the 7SK snRNA methyl phosphate capping enzyme (MEPCE) and La-related protein 7 (LARP7) stabilize the 7SK snRNA by adding a 5' methylphosphate cap or binding to the 3' poly(U) tail of the RNA, respectively (He et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Michels et al., 2004).

claim: MEPCE stabilizes the 7SK snRNA by adding a 5' methylphosphate cap.
source: In this complex, hexamethylene bisacetamide inducible 1 (HEXIM1) inhibits the kinase activity of CDK9 in a 7SK snRNA-dependent manner (Michels et al., 2004), while the 7SK snRNA methyl phosphate capping enzyme (MEPCE) and La-related protein 7 (LARP7) stabilize the 7SK snRNA by adding a 5' methylphosphate cap or binding to the 3' poly(U) tail of the RNA, respectively (He et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (He et al., 2008).

claim: LARP7 stabilizes the 7SK snRNA by binding to the 3' poly(U) tail of the RNA.
source: In this complex, hexamethylene bisacetamide inducible 1 (HEXIM1) inhibits the kinase activity of CDK9 in a 7SK snRNA-dependent manner (Michels et al., 2004), while the 7SK snRNA methyl phosphate capping enzyme (MEPCE) and La-related protein 7 (LARP7) stabilize the 7SK snRNA by adding a 5' methylphosphate cap or binding to the 3' poly(U) tail of the RNA, respectively (He et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (He et al., 2008).

claim: Multiple signaling pathways regulate the association of P-TEFb with the 7SK snRNP.
source: Multiple signaling pathways regulate the association of P-TEFb with the 7SK snRNP, tuning the required levels of active kinase in the cell (Chen et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014).

claim: 7SK snRNP-inhibited P-TEFb is recruited to the HIV-1 promoter.
source: We have previously shown that 7SK snRNP-inhibited P-TEFb is recruited to the HIV-1 promoter (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010), where Tat activates transcription elongation by displacing the inhibitory subunits through binding of the nascently transcribed transactivation response element (TAR) RNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010).

claim: Tat activates transcription elongation by displacing the inhibitory subunits through binding of the nascently transcribed TAR RNA.
source: We have previously shown that 7SK snRNP-inhibited P-TEFb is recruited to the HIV-1 promoter (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010), where Tat activates transcription elongation by displacing the inhibitory subunits through binding of the nascently transcribed transactivation response element (TAR) RNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010).

claim: snRNP-bound P-TEFb occupies the majority of promoters that display RNAP II pausing.
source: Supporting this model of activation, recent genome-wide studies have revealed that snRNP-bound P-TEFb occupies the majority of promoters that display RNAP II pausing (Ji et al., 2013; McNamara et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ji et al., 2013; McNamara et al., 2016).

claim: SC35 acts analogously to Tat by releasing the 7SK snRNP in a nascent RNA-binding-dependent step.
source: In this context, the splicing protein SC35 appears to act analogously to Tat by releasing the 7SK snRNP in a nascent RNA-binding-dependent step (Ji et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ji et al., 2013).

claim: Ubiquitin becomes covalently attached via its C-terminus to a primary amine on a substrate protein.
source: Ubiquitination is a post-translational modification in which the 76 amino acid protein ubiquitin becomes covalently attached via its C-terminus to a primary amine on a substrate protein.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ubiquitination.

claim: Mono-ubiquitination of histone H2B is associated with transcriptionally active chromatin and regulates subsequent histone modifications.
source: As an example, mono-ubiquitination of histone H2B is associated with transcriptionally active chromatin and regulates subsequent histone modifications (Hammond-Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hammond-Martel et al., 2012).

claim: Ubiquitination of p53 can lead to proteasomal degradation.
source: Ubiquitination of other transcription factors, including p53 and Myc, can lead to proteasomal degradation (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003), stabilization (Popov et al., 2010), or re-localization (Le Cam et al., 2006), underscoring the diversity of regulatory mechanisms for ubiquitination in transcriptional control.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003).

claim: Ubiquitination of Myc can lead to proteasomal degradation.
source: Ubiquitination of other transcription factors, including p53 and Myc, can lead to proteasomal degradation (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003), stabilization (Popov et al., 2010), or re-localization (Le Cam et al., 2006), underscoring the diversity of regulatory mechanisms for ubiquitination in transcriptional control.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003).

claim: Ubiquitination can lead to protein stabilization.
source: Ubiquitination of other transcription factors, including p53 and Myc, can lead to proteasomal degradation (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003), stabilization (Popov et al., 2010), or re-localization (Le Cam et al., 2006), underscoring the diversity of regulatory mechanisms for ubiquitination in transcriptional control.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Popov et al., 2010).

claim: Ubiquitination can lead to protein re-localization.
source: Ubiquitination of other transcription factors, including p53 and Myc, can lead to proteasomal degradation (Haupt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2003), stabilization (Popov et al., 2010), or re-localization (Le Cam et al., 2006), underscoring the diversity of regulatory mechanisms for ubiquitination in transcriptional control.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Le Cam et al., 2006).

claim: UBE2O is a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Here, we report the identification of ubiquitin conjugating enzyme E2 O (UBE2O), a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase (Mashtalir et al., 2014; Vila et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013a), as being critical for Tat transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mashtalir et al., 2014; Vila et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013a).

claim: Multiple independent siRNAs targeting ZFP91 inhibited Tat activity by 2-fold or greater.
source: Multiple independent siRNAs targeting ZFP91 or UBE2O inhibited Tat activity by 2-fold or greater, an effect similar to knockdown of the P-TEFb subunits CCNT1 and CDK9 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Multiple independent siRNAs targeting UBE2O inhibited Tat activity by 2-fold or greater.
source: Multiple independent siRNAs targeting ZFP91 or UBE2O inhibited Tat activity by 2-fold or greater, an effect similar to knockdown of the P-TEFb subunits CCNT1 and CDK9 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ZFP91 and UBE2O are expressed in CD4+ T cells.
source: Importantly, both ligases are expressed in CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), underscoring that they can regulate Tat activity during normal viral infection of target immune cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UBE2O knockdown significantly reduced the Tat-dependent production of distal, but not proximal, transcripts.
source: To determine whether ZFP91 and UBE2O specifically regulate transcription elongation, we measured promoter-proximal and -distal HIV-1 RNA production in the HeLaprovirusΔtat cells and found that UBE2O knockdown significantly reduced the Tat-dependent production of distal, but not proximal, transcripts (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: UBE2O was identified as a HEXIM1 interactor from multiple purifications.
source: Intriguingly, UBE2O was identified as a HEXIM1 interactor from multiple purifications (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The HEXIM1-UBE2O interaction was identified in a systematic AP-MS study of 2594 bait proteins.
source: The HEXIM1-UBE2O interaction was also identified in a recent effort to map the human interactome by systematic AP-MS of 2594 bait proteins (Huttlin et al., 2015), further validating the interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huttlin et al., 2015).

claim: HEXIM1 and UBE2O were identified in peak overlapping fractions from gel filtration of whole cell extracts.
source: As additional support for the interaction of HEXIM1 and UBE2O, both proteins were identified in peak overlapping fractions from gel filtration of whole cell extracts (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Tat dramatically increased the association between endogenous HEXIM1 and transfected UBE2O.
source: Tat dramatically increased the association between endogenous HEXIM1 and transfected UBE2O (Figure 1E), supporting the ability of a viral transcription factor to induce the binding between a ubiquitin ligase and a major transcriptional regulatory protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Tat, HEXIM1, and UBE2O can form a multi-protein complex.
source: We next performed a tandem affinity purification of Tat-STREP and UBE2O-FLAG followed by western blotting of endogenous HEXIM1, which demonstrated that these three proteins can form a multi-protein complex (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Tat forms an extensive interaction surface on the CCNT1 subunit of P-TEFb.
source: Tat forms an extensive interaction surface on the CCNT1 subunit of P-TEFb (Tahirov et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tahirov et al., 2010).

claim: A cluster of highly conserved, surface-exposed residues (Glu2, Tyr26, Lys28, and Phe32) displayed severe loss-of-function phenotypes and faced away from CCNT1 and CDK9.
source: In support of a distinct interaction surface, a cluster of highly conserved, surface-exposed residues (Glu2, Tyr26, Lys28, and Phe32) displayed severe loss-of-function phenotypes and faced away from CCNT1 and CDK9 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis and transcriptional activity data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tat K28A poorly bound to UBE2O and the 7SK snRNP proteins MEPCE and LARP7.
source: Indeed, Tat K28A poorly bound to UBE2O and the 7SK snRNP proteins MEPCE and LARP7 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for inputs).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The interactions of 7SK snRNP proteins with Tat is entirely RNA-dependent.
source: Of note, the interactions of these snRNP proteins with Tat is entirely RNA-dependent (Figure 2D, RNAse A treatment), implicating Lys28 in 7SK snRNA binding in addition to its role in modulating the TAR RNA interaction (D'Orso and Frankel, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAse A treatment data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutation of Phe32 (F32A) significantly increased binding to UBE2O by greater than 4-fold.
source: Strikingly, mutation of Phe32 (F32A), which is adjacent to Lys28 in the structure, significantly increased binding to UBE2O by greater than 4-fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The P-TEFb interaction was unaffected by Lys28 or Phe32 mutations.
source: Importantly, the P-TEFb interaction was unaffected by Lys28 or Phe32 mutations (Figure 2D), unlike the mutation of Phe38 (F38A) and Leu43 (L43A) residues that are buried in CCNT1 and disrupt P-TEFb binding, corroborating that Lys28 and Phe32 comprise a novel docking surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AFF1 is a ubiquitous P-TEFb binding partner.
source: The SEC scaffold protein, AFF1, had an identical binding profile to CDK9 and CCNT1, supporting recent work that AFF1 is a ubiquitous P-TEFb binding partner (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lu et al., 2014) and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: UBE2O co-expression dramatically increased HEXIM1 and MEPCE ubiquitination but not LARP7, CCNT1, or CDK9.
source: To test this, we first pulled down 7SK snRNP complex subunits and, upon blotting for transfected HA-tagged ubiquitin, found that UBE2O co-expression dramatically increased HEXIM1 and MEPCE ubiquitination but not LARP7, CCNT1, or CDK9 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MEPCE, but not LARP7, interacts with UBE2O.
source: Correlating with the ubiquitination results, AP-MS experiments with the LARP7 and MEPCE subunits identified MEPCE, but not LARP7, as interacting with UBE2O (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: HEXIM1 is known to be ubiquitinated.
source: As HEXIM1 is the key regulatory kinase inhibitor of the P-TEFb kinase (Michels et al., 2004) and is known to be ubiquitinated (Lau et al., 2009), we further characterized the HEXIM1 modification.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lau et al., 2009).

claim: Expression of a lysine-free ubiquitin mutant (Ub ΔK) did not affect UBE2O-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination in vivo.
source: Similar to previous studies, expression of a lysine-free ubiquitin mutant (Ub ΔK), which blocks the ability to form polyubiquitin chains, did not affect UBE2O-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination in vivo (Figure 3B), demonstrating that HEXIM1 is monoubiquitinated at multiple sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HEXIM1 is monoubiquitinated at multiple sites.
source: Similar to previous studies, expression of a lysine-free ubiquitin mutant (Ub ΔK), which blocks the ability to form polyubiquitin chains, did not affect UBE2O-dependent HEXIM1 ubiquitination in vivo (Figure 3B), demonstrating that HEXIM1 is monoubiquitinated at multiple sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A catalytically inactive mutant of UBE2O (C1040S or CD) did not ubiquitinate HEXIM1.
source: Further, a catalytically inactive mutant of UBE2O in the ubiquitin-conjugating domain (C1040S or CD) did not ubiquitinate HEXIM1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), supporting specific modification by UBE2O.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Wild-type UBE2O but not the CD mutant robustly modified HEXIM1 in vitro.
source: We next reconstituted ubiquitination of HEXIM1 by UBE2O in vitro and found that, like our observations in vivo, wild-type UBE2O but not the CD mutant robustly modified HEXIM1 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination of HEXIM1 was unaffected by treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: Indeed, UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination of HEXIM1 was unaffected by treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C showing MG132 control, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D showing extent of UBE2O overexpression), supporting a non-degradative mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data with MG132 treatment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tat expression increased HEXIM1 non-degradative mono-ubiquitination.
source: Strikingly, Tat expression increased HEXIM1 non-degradative mono-ubiquitination (Figure 3D), supporting a model of Tat-mediated HEXIM1 ubiquitination by UBE2O.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tat expression increased the ubiquitination of endogenous HEXIM1, but not CCNT1.
source: Tat expression also increased the ubiquitination of endogenous HEXIM1, but not CCNT1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), supporting the specificity of UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination as observed in transfected cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Endogenous HEXIM1 that is associated with Tat is in a modified state.
source: Furthermore, endogenous HEXIM1 that is associated with Tat, likely as part of the Tat-UBE2O-HEXIM1 complex (Figure 1F), is in a modified state (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), including a species with the same molecular weight as mono-ubiquitinated HEXIM1 (refer to Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Tat-stimulated non-degradative ubiquitination of endogenous HEXIM1 was completely blocked by siRNA-mediated knockdown of UBE2O.
source: Importantly, Tat-stimulated non-degradative ubiquitination of endogenous HEXIM1 (Figure 3E) was completely blocked by siRNA-mediated knockdown of UBE2O (Figure 3E), signifying that Tat hijacks the enzyme for HEXIM1 mono-ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data with UBE2O knockdown shown in Figure 3E.

claim: UBE2O knockdown prevented endogenous, Tat-independent HEXIM1 ubiquitination, but did not increase HEXIM1 protein levels.
source: In addition, UBE2O knockdown prevented endogenous, Tat-independent HEXIM1 ubiquitination, but did not increase HEXIM1 protein levels (Figure 3E), further confirming that HEXIM1 is an endogenous substrate for non-degradative UBE2O mono-ubiquitination, and is not an artifact of UBE2O overexpression.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HEXIM1 has a bipartite NLS composed of 12 and 3 basic amino acid segments surrounding a stretch of mostly aromatic hydrophobic (W, Y) amino acids.
source: Interestingly, while not identical, HEXIM1 has a similar motif (Figure 4A), with an NLS composed of 12 and 3 basic amino acid segments surrounding a stretch of mostly aromatic hydrophobic (W, Y) amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A fully lysine-free HEXIM1 mutant (ΔK) showed no modification.
source: To identify the sites of ubiquitination in HEXIM1 and to determine if the NLS is indeed a target, we first generated a fully lysine-free HEXIM1 mutant (ΔK) in which all lysines were mutated to arginine and observed no modification (Figure 4B, last lane), demonstrating that ubiquitination is lysine-dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When all lysines within the N- and C-termini were mutated to arginines (CTΔK + NTΔK), leaving lysines intact only within the NLS, HEXIM1 was still ubiquitinated.
source: When all lysines within the N- and C-termini were mutated to arginines (CTΔK + NTΔK), leaving lysines intact only within the NLS, HEXIM1 was still ubiquitinated (Figure 4B), consistent with acceptor residues being located in the NLS.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified multiple ubiquitinated lysines in the NLS and C-terminus of HEXIM1.
source: To more precisely map the acceptor sites, we used mass spectrometry (MS) and identified multiple ubiquitinated lysines in the NLS and C-terminus (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2), supporting our initial mapping (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Four lysines (Lys150, Lys151, Lys152, and Lys159) in the HEXIM1 NLS recovered monoubiquitination, with Lys151 and Lys159 being the most robust.
source: Therefore, as an alternative approach to map acceptor sites in the NLS, we restored individual lysines within the lysine-free (ΔK) background and found that four (Lys150, Lys151, Lys152, and Lys159) recovered monoubiquitination, with Lys151 and Lys159 being the most robust (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A HEXIM1 mutant deficient for 7SK RNA binding (150–156 Ala) displayed a complete loss of UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination.
source: In support of this model, a HEXIM1 mutant deficient for 7SK RNA binding (150–156 Ala) (Michels et al., 2004; Yik et al., 2004) displayed a complete loss of UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination, in striking contrast to another HEXIM1 mutant deficient for P-TEFb binding that was still fully ubiquitinated (202PYNT205 -> 202PDND205) (Michels et al., 2004) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A HEXIM1 mutant deficient for P-TEFb binding (202PYNT205 -> 202PDND205) was still fully ubiquitinated.
source: In support of this model, a HEXIM1 mutant deficient for 7SK RNA binding (150–156 Ala) (Michels et al., 2004; Yik et al., 2004) displayed a complete loss of UBE2O-dependent ubiquitination, in striking contrast to another HEXIM1 mutant deficient for P-TEFb binding that was still fully ubiquitinated (202PYNT205 -> 202PDND205) (Michels et al., 2004) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A HEXIM1 150–156 Arg mutant which retains RNA binding was ubiquitinated equally to wild-type HEXIM1.
source: Because the 150–156 Ala mutant also lacks some of the lysines that become ubiquitinated (Figure 4D), we generated a HEXIM1 150–156 Arg mutant which similarly lacks the NLS acceptor lysines but retains RNA binding (Lau et al., 2009) and found that it was ubiquitinated equally to wild-type HEXIM1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RNA binding by HEXIM1 appears to be a prerequisite for UBE2O recognition and ubiquitination.
source: Thus, RNA binding by HEXIM1 appears to be a prerequisite for UBE2O recognition and ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that RNA-binding deficient HEXIM1 mutants are not ubiquitinated (Figure 4E).

claim: 7SK RNA-binding releases HEXIM1 from an auto-inhibited state.
source: 7SK RNA-binding releases HEXIM1 from an auto-inhibited state (Barboric et al., 2005), which likely establishes the proper conformation of HEXIM1 for UBE2O ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Barboric et al., 2005).

claim: Expression of UBE2O altered the localization of endogenous HEXIM1 with an increase of HEXIM1 in the cytoplasm and a simultaneous decrease in the nuclear pellet fraction containing chromatin.
source: Expression of UBE2O, itself a cytoplasmic ubiquitin ligase, altered the localization of endogenous HEXIM1 with an increase of HEXIM1 in the cytoplasm and a simultaneous decrease in the nuclear pellet fraction containing chromatin (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of the UBE2O-dependent ubiquitinated species of HEXIM1 were cytoplasmic.
source: Consistent with the cytoplasmic accumulation of HEXIM1, the majority of the UBE2O-dependent ubiquitinated species of HEXIM1 were also cytoplasmic (Figure 5B, lane 2), suggesting that HEXIM1 may be ubiquitinated in this fraction to regulate its localization and inhibit chromatin recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and ubiquitination data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The lysine-free HEXIM1ΔK mutant accumulated greater than threefold more in the chromatin-containing nuclear pellet compared to wild-type HEXIM1.
source: Interestingly, the lysine-free HEXIM1ΔK mutant, which is not ubiquitinated by UBE2O (Figure 4B), accumulated greater than threefold more in the chromatin-containing nuclear pellet compared to wild-type HEXIM1 when expressed in HEK 293 T cells (Figure 5C), further supporting a role of HEXIM1 lysine modification in regulating its localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The knockdown of UBE2O resulted in an increased association of CCNT1, CDK9, and LARP7 with endogenously purified HEXIM1.
source: Interestingly, the knockdown of UBE2O resulted in an increased association of CCNT1, CDK9, and LARP7 with endogenously purified HEXIM1 (Figure 6A), with no obvious effect on the HEXIM1 interactions with proteins of the NEAT1 RNP.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UBE2O knockdown had no obvious effect on the HEXIM1 interactions with proteins of the NEAT1 RNP.
source: Interestingly, the knockdown of UBE2O resulted in an increased association of CCNT1, CDK9, and LARP7 with endogenously purified HEXIM1 (Figure 6A), with no obvious effect on the HEXIM1 interactions with proteins of the NEAT1 RNP.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tat expression released HEXIM1 from the 7SK snRNP, with no effect on NEAT1 RNP interactions.
source: Further, while Tat expression released HEXIM1 from the 7SK snRNP, with no effect on NEAT1 RNP interactions (Figure 6A), knockdown of UBE2O limited the ability of Tat to disrupt HEXIM1-CCNT1 binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of UBE2O limited the ability of Tat to disrupt HEXIM1-CCNT1 binding.
source: Further, while Tat expression released HEXIM1 from the 7SK snRNP, with no effect on NEAT1 RNP interactions (Figure 6A), knockdown of UBE2O limited the ability of Tat to disrupt HEXIM1-CCNT1 binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Tat F32A mutant was unable to stimulate HEXIM1 ubiquitination.
source: Unlike wild-type Tat, the F32A mutant was unable to stimulate HEXIM1 ubiquitination (Figure 6B) despite its increased association with UBE2O (Figure 2D), further supporting a non-productive binding mode of this Tat mutant to the ligase.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Tat F32A mutant was deficient in releasing P-TEFb from endogenous 7SK snRNP-bound HEXIM1 compared to wild type Tat.
source: Further, the F32A mutant was deficient in releasing P-TEFb from endogenous 7SK snRNP-bound HEXIM1 compared to wild type Tat (Figure 6C), corroborating a role for HEXIM1 ubiquitination in the P-TEFb eviction step by Tat.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The HEXIM1 ΔK mutant was refractory to complete P-TEFb release by Tat compared to wild-type HEXIM1.
source: This lysine-free mutant was refractory to complete P-TEFb release by Tat (Figure 6D) compared to wild-type HEXIM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A native IP of endogenous HEXIM1 from cytoplasmic and soluble nuclear fractions revealed robust RNA-dependent interactions between HEXIM1 and proteins of the P-TEFb-7SK snRNP complex in the cytoplasm.
source: Indeed, a native IP of endogenous HEXIM1 from cytoplasmic and soluble nuclear fractions revealed robust RNA-dependent interactions between HEXIM1 and proteins of the P-TEFb-7SK snRNP complex in the cytoplasm (Figure 7A), agreeing with a previous finding that a significant fraction of a 'large-form' of P-TEFb is in the cytoplasm (Ramanathan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A significant fraction of a 'large-form' of P-TEFb is in the cytoplasm.
source: Indeed, a native IP of endogenous HEXIM1 from cytoplasmic and soluble nuclear fractions revealed robust RNA-dependent interactions between HEXIM1 and proteins of the P-TEFb-7SK snRNP complex in the cytoplasm (Figure 7A), agreeing with a previous finding that a significant fraction of a 'large-form' of P-TEFb is in the cytoplasm (Ramanathan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ramanathan et al., 1999).

claim: Immunofluorescence confirmed that a significant fraction of the CCNT1 subunit of P-TEFb was localized to the cytoplasm.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed that a significant fraction of the CCNT1 subunit of P-TEFb was localized to the cytoplasm (Figure 7B), consistent with a previous observation that CCNT1 and CDK9 are detected in the cytoplasm in unstimulated resting memory CD4+ T cells, the target immune cells of HIV-1 infection (Mbonye et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CCNT1 and CDK9 are detected in the cytoplasm in unstimulated resting memory CD4+ T cells.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed that a significant fraction of the CCNT1 subunit of P-TEFb was localized to the cytoplasm (Figure 7B), consistent with a previous observation that CCNT1 and CDK9 are detected in the cytoplasm in unstimulated resting memory CD4+ T cells, the target immune cells of HIV-1 infection (Mbonye et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mbonye et al., 2013).

claim: The interaction of HEXIM1 with 7SK snRNA was detected in the cytoplasm.
source: Further, the interaction of HEXIM1 with 7SK snRNA was also detected in the cytoplasm (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-IP data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tat expressed in HeLa cells decreased the amount of CCNT1 and CDK9 in the cytoplasm four-fold with a concomitant increase in the nuclear, chromatin-containing pellet.
source: Indeed, Tat expressed in HeLa cells, which we observed in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions (Figure 7D, STREP western), decreased the amount of CCNT1 and CDK9 in the cytoplasm four-fold with a concomitant increase in the nuclear, chromatin-containing pellet (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Localization of HEXIM1 was unaltered by Tat expression.
source: Notably, localization of HEXIM1, of which nearly 30% is in complex with P-TEFb in HeLa cells (Barboric et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2005), was unaltered, supporting that free, and not snRNP-bound, P-TEFb enters the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Nearly 30% of HEXIM1 is in complex with P-TEFb in HeLa cells.
source: Notably, localization of HEXIM1, of which nearly 30% is in complex with P-TEFb in HeLa cells (Barboric et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2005), was unaltered, supporting that free, and not snRNP-bound, P-TEFb enters the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Barboric et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2005).

claim: Tat expression increased the enrichment of CDK9 at the viral promoter.
source: As expected, Tat expression increased the enrichment of CDK9 at the viral promoter (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Knockdown of UBE2O greatly inhibited Tat-dependent CDK9 recruitment to the integrated viral promoter.
source: Importantly, knockdown of UBE2O greatly inhibited Tat-dependent CDK9 recruitment to the integrated viral promoter, supporting a critical role of this ligase in regulating viral transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: UBE2O knockdown prevented CDK9 enrichment in the absence of Tat.
source: UBE2O knockdown also prevented CDK9 enrichment in the absence of Tat, supporting an endogenous role of UBE2O in regulating HEXIM1 ubiquitination and maintaining appropriate P-TEFb kinase levels on the HIV-1 promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: DRB blocks transcription elongation by decreasing RNAP II serine two phosphorylation (S2-P).
source: Viruses often hijack existing host mechanisms; therefore, to investigate whether the nuclear import of P-TEFb freed from cytoplasmic 7SK snRNP might be a more general pathway to regulate transcriptional elongation, we used the CDK7/9 inhibitor 5,6-Dichloro-1-beta-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB), which blocks transcription elongation by decreasing RNAP II serine two phosphorylation (S2-P) (Koga et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Koga et al., 2015).

claim: RNAP II S2-P levels dramatically decreased when HeLa cells were treated with DRB.
source: RNAP II S2-P levels dramatically decreased when HeLa cells were treated with DRB (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: DRB treatment induced extensive re-localization of P-TEFb, but not HEXIM1, from the cytoplasm to the nuclear pellet.
source: Remarkably, similar to Tat, DRB treatment induced extensive re-localization of P-TEFb, but not HEXIM1, from the cytoplasm to the nuclear pellet, the same fraction containing reduced RNAP II S2-P.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: DRB treatment increased the association between UBE2O and endogenous HEXIM1.
source: Supporting a role of UBE2O in this import pathway, DRB treatment also increased the association between UBE2O and endogenous HEXIM1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: UBE2O ubiquitinates multiple chromatin-associated proteins within their nuclear localization signal, resulting in cytoplasmic retention.
source: UBE2O is a hybrid E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase that can ubiquitinate multiple chromatin-associated proteins within their nuclear localization signal (NLS), resulting in cytoplasmic retention (Mashtalir et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mashtalir et al., 2014).

claim: UBE2O induces the degradation of the mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) protein.
source: UBE2O has also recently been shown to induce the degradation of the mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) protein, which is commonly fused to members of the P-TEFb-based super elongation complex in leukemia (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Liang et al., 2017).

claim: ZFP91 ubiquitinates NF-κB-inducing kinase via a Lys63 linkage to activate a non-canonical NF-κB pathway.
source: ZFP91 ubiquitinates NF-κB-inducing kinase via a Lys63 linkage to activate a non-canonical NF-κB pathway (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jin et al., 2010).

claim: Newly translated Tat is cytoplasmic, especially during acute infection.
source: Since newly translated Tat is cytoplasmic, especially during acute infection (Ranki et al., 1994; Kim et al., 2010), and shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm (Stauber and Pavlakis, 1998), we reasoned Tat might alter the localization of P-TEFb.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ranki et al., 1994; Kim et al., 2010).

claim: Tat shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Since newly translated Tat is cytoplasmic, especially during acute infection (Ranki et al., 1994; Kim et al., 2010), and shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm (Stauber and Pavlakis, 1998), we reasoned Tat might alter the localization of P-TEFb.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Stauber and Pavlakis, 1998).

claim: P-TEFb nuclear import can be observed at the lowest Tat expression levels tested.
source: P-TEFb nuclear import can be observed at the lowest Tat expression levels tested, arguing against an overexpression phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: HIV-1 has a small 9-kilobase genome encoding only 18 proteins.
source: Since HIV-1 has a small 9-kilobase genome encoding only 18 proteins, it has evolved ways to economically utilize its limited genetic information and rely heavily on host protein complexes to execute all stages of its life cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about HIV-1.

claim: High FRET signal between Tat and CCNT1 in the cytoplasm supports the hypothesis that Tat can utilize the cytoplasmic pool of inhibited P-TEFb.
source: High FRET signal between Tat and CCNT1 in the cytoplasm (Marcello et al., 2001) and an intrinsic nucleocytoplasmic shuttling activity of CDK9 (Napolitano et al., 2002) support this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Marcello et al., 2001).

claim: CDK9 has an intrinsic nucleocytoplasmic shuttling activity.
source: High FRET signal between Tat and CCNT1 in the cytoplasm (Marcello et al., 2001) and an intrinsic nucleocytoplasmic shuttling activity of CDK9 (Napolitano et al., 2002) support this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Napolitano et al., 2002).

claim: UBE2O inhibits NF-κB activation by preventing the polyubiquitination of TRAF6.
source: Intriguingly, UBE2O inhibits NF-κB activation by preventing the polyubiquitination of TRAF6 (Zhang et al., 2013b), suggesting that UBE2O is potentially intercalated in a signaling pathway that regulates stimulus-dependent NF-κB and P-TEFb nuclear import.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2013b).

claim: ZFP91 is a classical C2H2 zinc finger protein.
source: ZFP91 is a classical C2H2 zinc finger (ZnF) protein, and while ZnF domains generally function as DNA-binding motifs, a previous report demonstrated that one ZFP91 ZnF domain can function as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ZFP91.

claim: One ZFP91 ZnF domain can function as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: ZFP91 is a classical C2H2 zinc finger (ZnF) protein, and while ZnF domains generally function as DNA-binding motifs, a previous report demonstrated that one ZFP91 ZnF domain can function as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jin et al., 2010).

claim: The P-TEFb-7SK snRNP complex is recruited to the HIV-1 promoter in its basal state (without Tat), resulting in P-TEFb inhibition and accumulation of paused RNA polymerase II at the promoter.
source: As shown previously (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010), the P-TEFb-7SK snRNP complex is recruited to the HIV-1 promoter in its basal state (without Tat), resulting in P-TEFb inhibition and accumulation of paused RNA polymerase II at the promoter, consequently poising the system for activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010).

claim: UBE2O ubiquitinates nuclear and cytoplasmic HEXIM1, sequestering HEXIM1 in the cytoplasm and releasing some P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP for nuclear import and retention.
source: In addition, UBE2O ubiquitinates nuclear and cytoplasmic HEXIM1, sequestering HEXIM1 in the cytoplasm and releasing some P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP for nuclear import and retention.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including subcellular fractionation and ubiquitination assays.

claim: UBE2O activity supports basal, low-level HIV-1 gene expression.
source: This activity of UBE2O supports basal, low-level HIV-1 gene expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing UBE2O's role in regulating P-TEFb and HEXIM1.

claim: Once Tat is expressed, it can assemble with the inhibited P-TEFb complex at the HIV-1 promoter.
source: Once Tat is expressed, it can assemble with the inhibited P-TEFb complex at the HIV-1 promoter.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Tat function.

claim: The synthesis of TAR RNA results in the displacement of the inhibitory snRNP to activate the kinase activity of CDK9.
source: The synthesis of TAR RNA results in the displacement of the inhibitory snRNP to activate the kinase activity of CDK9 (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (D'Orso and Frankel, 2010).

claim: Tat enhances the association of UBE2O with HEXIM1, leading to increased HEXIM1 ubiquitination and P-TEFb release and nuclear import.
source: Further, Tat enhances the association of UBE2O with HEXIM1, leading to increased HEXIM1 ubiquitination and P-TEFb release and nuclear import.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assays.

claim: Residue F32 in Tat is critically important for the UBE2O-dependent activation mechanism.
source: Residue F32 in Tat is critically important for the UBE2O-dependent activation mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that the F32A mutant is defective in stimulating HEXIM1 ubiquitination and P-TEFb release.

claim: Tat targets both the nuclear and cytoplasmic pools of the 7SK snRNP complex.
source: Tat appears to target both the nuclear and cytoplasmic pools of the 7SK snRNP complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Tat's effects on both nuclear and cytoplasmic P-TEFb.

claim: P-TEFb that is released from the cytoplasmic pool enters the nucleus to sustain high-level transcriptional activation in Tat-expressing cells.
source: P-TEFb that is released from the cytoplasmic pool enters the nucleus to sustain high-level transcriptional activation in Tat-expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing P-TEFb redistribution upon Tat expression.

claim: As Tat expression levels increase, more of the cytoplasmic P-TEFb reservoir is utilized.
source: However, work presented here demonstrates that as Tat expression levels increase, more of the cytoplasmic P-TEFb reservoir is utilized, as evidenced by the dose response of Tat protein levels and the increase in P-TEFb nuclear import (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The nuclear import of free P-TEFb kinase is a more general regulatory mechanism that is not restricted to HIV-1 transcription.
source: Given that DRB, a compound that induces stress and thus 7SK snRNP disassembly, also increases P-TEFb nuclear import and retention, it may be likely that the nuclear import of free P-TEFb kinase is a more general regulatory mechanism that is not restricted to HIV-1 transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing DRB's effects on P-TEFb localization.
